::: {.solutions}

The [Sequences & Series clinic](class_material.qmd) covers **MM2 as written**. This page covers everything
the mocks throw at you that MM2 does **not** list.

::: {.callout-important}
## The whole point of this page

Here is **every** series result the specification actually gives you:

> **MM2.1** sequences from an $n$th-term formula or a simple recurrence $x_{n+1}=\mathrm{f}(x_n)$
> **MM2.2** arithmetic series, **including the formula for the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers**
> **MM2.3** the sum of a finite geometric series; the sum to infinity of a **convergent** one, $|r|<1$
> **M4.19** deduce the $n$th term of **linear or quadratic** sequences

That is it. $\displaystyle\sum k^{2}$, $\displaystyle\sum k^{3}$, $\displaystyle\sum k\,2^{k}$ and
$\displaystyle\sum\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ are **not on the list** — yet all four appear in the JZ mocks and in the
harder past papers.

[So you are never expected to *recall* them. You are expected to *build* them]{.hl}, and there are only
three construction methods. Learn the three and no series question can be unfamiliar.
:::

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">Beyond MM2 · the three ways to build a sum</div>
<div class="fs-title">Series Construction Methods</div>
<div class="fs-sub">When the formula is not on the sheet, one of these three produces it.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### A · [Method of differences (telescoping)]{.hl}
If you can write $u_k=\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1)$, then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_k=\mathrm{f}(1)-\mathrm{f}(n+1)$$
and everything in between cancels. **Partial fractions** is how you get that form.
[$\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### B · [The shifted copy]{.hl}
For $S=\sum k\,r^{k}$, write $rS$ underneath $S$ so the powers line up, then subtract. The $k$ collapses
and what is left is geometric.
[$\sum_{k=1}^{20}k\,2^{k}=19\cdot2^{21}+2$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### C · [Sum an identity]{.hl}
To get $\sum k^{2}$, sum the identity $(k+1)^{3}-k^{3}=3k^{2}+3k+1$. The left side telescopes, and
rearranging gives the answer.
[the same trick with $k^{4}$ gives $\sum k^{3}$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The three power sums
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\quad\text{\small(on the spec)}$$
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$$
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{3}=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^{2}$$
[$\sum k^{3}=\left(\sum k\right)^{2}$ — worth remembering]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Two ways a $\sum$ to infinity can exist
**Geometric:** $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, needs $\lvert r\rvert<1$.
**Telescoping:** the partial sum is $\mathrm{f}(1)-\mathrm{f}(n+1)$, so $S_\infty=\mathrm{f}(1)-\lim
\mathrm{f}(n+1)$.
[UK courses teach only the first; the mocks use both]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Quadratic sequences
**Constant second difference** $\iff$ $n$th term is $an^{2}+bn+c$, and
$$2a=\text{the second difference.}$$
Then fit $b,c$ from the first two terms.
[$2,7,16,29,46\to 2n^{2}-n+1$]{.eg}
:::

# 1 · Quadratic sequences and the power sums

## Finding the $n$th term of a quadratic sequence

This part **is** on the specification (M4.19), and it is the cheapest mark in the topic.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Second differences give the leading coefficient

A sequence has $n$th term $an^{2}+bn+c$ **exactly when** its second differences are constant, and then

$$\boxed{\,2a=\text{the (constant) second difference}\,}$$

*Why: the first difference of $an^{2}+bn+c$ is $a(2n+1)+b$, which is linear in $n$ with gradient $2a$; the
difference of that is $2a$.*
:::

**Method.**

1. Write the first differences, then the second differences.
2. Halve the second difference to get $a$.
3. Subtract $an^{2}$ from the sequence — what is left is **arithmetic**, and gives $b$ and $c$.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Find the $n$th term of $2,\ 7,\ 16,\ 29,\ 46,\ \dots$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

| | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sequence | $2$ | $7$ | $16$ | $29$ | $46$ |
| 1st differences | | $5$ | $9$ | $13$ | $17$ |
| 2nd differences | | | $4$ | $4$ | $4$ |

Constant second difference $4$, so $2a=4$ and $a=2$. Subtract $2n^{2}$:

| $n$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $u_n-2n^{2}$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $-2$ | $-3$ | $-4$ |

which is arithmetic with $n$th term $1-n$. Hence

$$u_n=2n^{2}-n+1 .$$

**Check:** $n=5$ gives $50-5+1=46$ ✓
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Building $\sum k^{2}$ — method C

You are given $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and nothing else. Here is how $\sum k^{2}$
comes out of it in four lines.

**Start from an identity that produces $k^{2}$ when expanded:**

$$(k+1)^{3}-k^{3}=3k^{2}+3k+1 .$$

**Sum both sides from $k=1$ to $n$.** The left side **telescopes** — write it out and watch:

$$\underbrace{\left(2^{3}-1^{3}\right)+\left(3^{3}-2^{3}\right)+\cdots+\left((n+1)^{3}-n^{3}\right)}_{\text{everything cancels but the ends}}=(n+1)^{3}-1 .$$

**So**

$$(n+1)^{3}-1=3\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}+3\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+n .$$

**Rearrange.** Expanding the left as $n^{3}+3n^{2}+3n$:

$$3\sum k^{2}=n^{3}+3n^{2}+3n-\frac{3n(n+1)}{2}-n=\frac{2n^{3}+3n^{2}+n}{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{2},$$

$$\boxed{\ \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\ }$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## The same trick for $\sum k^{3}$ — try it first

Start from $(k+1)^{4}-k^{4}=4k^{3}+6k^{2}+4k+1$ and sum from $1$ to $n$:

$$(n+1)^{4}-1=4\sum k^{3}+6\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+4\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+n .$$

Rearranging gives

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{3}=\frac{n^{2}(n+1)^{2}}{4}=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^{2}=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\right)^{2}.$$

**Check at $n=3$:** $1+8+27=36$ and $\left(\tfrac{3\cdot4}{2}\right)^{2}=6^{2}=36$ ✓

*Each power sum is built from the ones below it, which is why the order matters: $\sum k$, then $\sum k^{2}$,
then $\sum k^{3}$.*
:::

**Consequence.** Any sum of a **polynomial** in $k$ is now routine — split it term by term:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(3k^{2}-2k+5\right)=3\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+5n .$$

# 2 · The method of differences (telescoping)

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the one that is not in the UK course

A British A-level student meets $\sum$ **to infinity** only through the geometric series, so a sum like
$\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ looks impossible — it is not geometric, and no formula
applies. The technique below is standard in the Korean curriculum (*부분급수* / partial sums) and in
Further Maths, and **JZ Mock A Paper 2 Q8 is exactly this**.

It is not hard. It is one idea.
:::

## The idea

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method of differences

If the term can be written as a **difference of consecutive values of one function**,

$$u_k=\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1),$$

then adding from $k=1$ to $n$ cancels everything in the middle:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_k=\Big(\mathrm{f}(1)-\cancel{\mathrm{f}(2)}\Big)+\Big(\cancel{\mathrm{f}(2)}-\cancel{\mathrm{f}(3)}\Big)+\cdots+\Big(\cancel{\mathrm{f}(n)}-\mathrm{f}(n+1)\Big)
=\mathrm{f}(1)-\mathrm{f}(n+1).$$

**Only the ends survive.** And then

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}u_k=\mathrm{f}(1)-\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{f}(n+1),$$

which exists whenever that limit does.
:::

## Getting the term into that form: partial fractions

Method: split the fraction, then check the pieces really are consecutive.

| term | split | gap | what survives |
|---|---|:-:|---|
| $\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}$ | $\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}$ | $1$ | **one** term at each end |
| $\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}$ | $\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+2}\right)$ | $2$ | **two** terms at each end |
| $\dfrac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}$ | $\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{2k-1}-\dfrac1{2k+1}\right)$ | $1$ | one at each end |

[The gap is the thing to check]{.hl}. With a gap of $2$, the cancellation skips a term, so $\mathrm{f}(1)$
**and** $\mathrm{f}(2)$ both survive at the front — and two survive at the back as well.

::: {.example}
[Example 1.]{.lbl} Find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ and hence $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

$$\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\qquad\text{(check: } \tfrac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}=\tfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\text{ ✓)}$$

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\right)
=\left(1-\frac12\right)+\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right)
=1-\frac{1}{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}.$$

**Partial sums:** $\tfrac12,\ \tfrac23,\ \tfrac34,\ \tfrac45,\dots$ — the pattern alone tells you the limit.

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}=1 .$$
:::

::: {.example}
[Example 2 — the gap-2 case.]{.lbl} Find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

$$\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1k-\frac1{k+2}\right).$$

Writing out the first few and the last few, **two** terms survive at each end:

$$2\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\underbrace{\frac11+\frac12}_{\text{front}}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{n+2}}_{\text{back}} .$$

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac32-\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{n+2}\right)
\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\;\frac12\cdot\frac32=\boxed{\frac34}.$$

**Check numerically:** the first six terms give $0.7202\ldots$, the first fifty $0.7452\ldots$ — creeping up
to $0.75$ ✓

*Answering $\tfrac12$ here, by assuming one term survives at each end, is the standard error. **Write out
three terms from each end before cancelling.***
:::

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.0))
N = np.arange(1, 26)

part = np.cumsum(1/(N*(N+1)))
axes[0].plot(N, part, 'o-', color='#1f77b4', ms=4, lw=1.6)
axes[0].axhline(1, color='#d62728', lw=1.6, ls='--')
axes[0].text(25, 1.03, 'limit $1$', color='#d62728', ha='right', fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_title('$\\sum \\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$  — telescoping\npartial sum is $\\frac{n}{n+1}$',
                  fontsize=11)

geo = np.cumsum(0.5**N)
axes[1].plot(N, geo, 'o-', color='#2ca02c', ms=4, lw=1.6)
axes[1].axhline(1, color='#d62728', lw=1.6, ls='--')
axes[1].text(25, 1.03, 'limit $1$', color='#d62728', ha='right', fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_title('$\\sum \\left(\\frac{1}{2}\\right)^{k}$  — geometric\npartial sum is $1-2^{-n}$',
                  fontsize=11)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1.18); ax.set_xlabel('number of terms $n$')
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*Both sums converge to $1$, and for the same underlying reason — **the partial sum has a closed form whose
limit you can read off**. The geometric one you are taught; the telescoping one you build.*

## The mock question this was set for

::: {.example}
[JZ Mock A · Paper 2 · Q8.]{.lbl} A sequence has $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}=\dfrac{a_n}{1+a_n}$ for $n\ge1$.
Find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_na_{n+1}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0$ &nbsp; **B** $1$ &nbsp; **C** $2$ &nbsp; **D** $4$ &nbsp; **E** $\tfrac52$ &nbsp;
**F** $\tfrac32$ &nbsp; **G** $\infty$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B** $\;1$

**Step 1 — the recurrence (this part is in-spec, MM2.1).** A recurrence that *divides* by something
involving $a_n$ is almost always linear in the **reciprocal**:

$$a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{1+a_n}\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{1}{a_{n+1}}=\frac{1+a_n}{a_n}=\frac{1}{a_n}+1 .$$

So $b_n=\dfrac{1}{a_n}$ is **arithmetic** with $b_1=1$ and common difference $1$, giving $b_n=n$ and

$$a_n=\frac1n .$$

*(If you did not spot the reciprocal: computing $a_1=1,\ a_2=\tfrac12,\ a_3=\tfrac13$ suggests it in ten
seconds, and the recurrence then confirms it.)*

**Step 2 — the sum (this is the off-spec part).**

$$a_na_{n+1}=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+1},$$

which is Example 1 above:

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_na_{n+1}=1 .$$

**Why this felt impossible.** The sum is not geometric, so the one $S_\infty$ formula on the specification
does not apply — and nothing else on the specification does either. [The move that unlocks it is splitting
the fraction so that consecutive terms cancel]{.hl}, and once you have seen it once it is never hard again.
:::

# 3 · The shifted copy — sums like $\sum k\,r^{k}$

A sum whose term is **a polynomial times a geometric term** is neither arithmetic nor geometric, so no
formula applies. The fix is to **subtract a shifted copy of the sum from itself**, which collapses the
polynomial factor.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method

For $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\,r^{k}$, write $rS$ so that equal powers line up, and subtract. Each
$k\,r^{k}-(k-1)r^{k}=r^{k}$, so what is left is a plain **geometric** series plus the two end terms.
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}k\,2^{k}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Let $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}k\,2^{k}$. Then

$$2S=\sum_{k=1}^{20}k\,2^{k+1}=\sum_{j=2}^{21}(j-1)\,2^{j}.$$

Subtract, lining up equal powers of $2$:

$$S=2S-S=\underbrace{20\cdot2^{21}}_{j=21\text{ only in }2S}-\underbrace{1\cdot2^{1}}_{k=1\text{ only in }S}-\sum_{j=2}^{20}2^{j}.$$

The remaining sum is geometric: $\displaystyle\sum_{j=2}^{20}2^{j}=2^{21}-4$. Hence

$$S=20\cdot2^{21}-2-\left(2^{21}-4\right)=19\cdot2^{21}+2 .$$

**Check:** $19\cdot2^{21}+2=39\,845\,890$, and summing directly gives the same. ✓

*This is **JZ Mock B Paper 1 Q19** almost verbatim — there it is wrapped in a ceiling function, but
$\lceil x\rceil=k$ on $(k-1,k]$ turns the integral into exactly this sum.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## The infinite version

For $\lvert x\rvert<1$ the same subtraction gives

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k\,x^{k}=\frac{x}{(1-x)^{2}} .$$

*Derivation:* $S-xS=\sum_{k\ge1}x^{k}=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$, so $S(1-x)=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$.

**Check at $x=\tfrac12$:** $\dfrac{1/2}{1/4}=2$, and $\tfrac12+\tfrac24+\tfrac38+\tfrac4{16}+\cdots$ does
climb to $2$ ✓
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

# 4 · Which method?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Read the term, pick the method

| the term $u_k$ looks like | method | result |
|---|---|---|
| $a+(k-1)d$ — linear in $k$ | arithmetic formula | *on the spec* |
| $a\,r^{k}$ | geometric formula | *on the spec* |
| a **polynomial** in $k$ | split into $\sum k^{2},\sum k,\sum 1$ | build $\sum k^{2}$ by method C |
| a **fraction that splits** into consecutive pieces | method of differences | Part 2 |
| $k\,r^{k}$ — polynomial $\times$ geometric | the shifted copy | Part 3 |
| already given as $\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1)$ | method of differences, immediately | Part 2 |
:::

**And one warning that applies to all of them.** A sum to infinity exists only if the **partial sum** has a
limit. For a geometric series that is the condition $\lvert r\rvert<1$; for a telescoping series it is
$\lim\mathrm{f}(n+1)$ existing. *Never write $S_\infty$ without saying why the limit is there.*

# 5 · Practice

## Question 1

::: {.question}
Find the $n$th term of $\;5,\ 12,\ 23,\ 38,\ 57,\ \dots$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

First differences $7,11,15,19$; second differences $4,4,4$. So $2a=4$, $a=2$.

Subtracting $2n^{2}$ gives $3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6,\ 7$, which is $n+2$. Hence

$$u_n=2n^{2}+n+2 .$$

**Check** $n=4$: $32+4+2=38$ ✓
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(k^{2}-3k\right)$, giving a single factorised expression.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}-3\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-\frac{3n(n+1)}{2}
=\frac{n(n+1)}{6}\Big[(2n+1)-9\Big]=\frac{n(n+1)(2n-8)}{6}=\frac{n(n+1)(n-4)}{3}.$$

**Check** $n=3$: $(1-3)+(4-6)+(9-9)=-4$, and $\tfrac{3\cdot4\cdot(-1)}{3}=-4$ ✓
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\frac{n}{2n+1}$, and write down the sum to
infinity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

$$\frac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\frac12\left(\frac{1}{2k-1}-\frac{1}{2k+1}\right)$$

*(check: $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{(2k+1)-(2k-1)}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\tfrac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}$ ✓)*

The pieces are consecutive, so one survives at each end:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}=\frac12\left(\frac11-\frac{1}{2n+1}\right)=\frac12\cdot\frac{2n}{2n+1}=\frac{n}{2n+1}. \;\blacksquare$$

$$S_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{2n+1}=\frac12 .$$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
A sequence satisfies $u_1=\tfrac12$ and $u_{n+1}=\dfrac{u_n}{2u_n+1}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Find a formula for $u_n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}u_nu_{n+1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(a)** Take reciprocals:

$$\frac{1}{u_{n+1}}=\frac{2u_n+1}{u_n}=\frac{1}{u_n}+2 ,$$

so $\tfrac1{u_n}$ is arithmetic with first term $2$ and common difference $2$: $\tfrac1{u_n}=2n$, giving

$$u_n=\frac{1}{2n}.$$

**(b)**

$$u_nu_{n+1}=\frac{1}{4n(n+1)}=\frac14\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right),$$

so by Example 1 the sum is $\tfrac14\times1=\boxed{\tfrac14}$.

*The same two steps as the JZ question: reciprocal to solve the recurrence, then telescope.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}k\,3^{k}$, leaving your answer in the form $a\cdot3^{11}+b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Let $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}k\,3^{k}$, so $3S=\displaystyle\sum_{j=2}^{11}(j-1)3^{j}$. Subtracting,

$$2S=3S-S=10\cdot3^{11}-3-\sum_{j=2}^{10}3^{j} .$$

The geometric part is $\displaystyle\sum_{j=2}^{10}3^{j}=\frac{3^{11}-9}{2}$, so

$$2S=10\cdot3^{11}-3-\frac{3^{11}-9}{2}=\frac{19\cdot3^{11}+3}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad S=\frac{19}{4}\cdot3^{11}+\frac34 .$$

**Check:** $S=841\,674$, and $\tfrac{19}{4}\cdot177147+\tfrac34=841\,673.25+0.75=841\,674$ ✓

*With $r=3$ the subtraction gives $2S$, not $S$ — always write down which multiple you have produced.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Explain why $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}$ **cannot** be found by the method of differences
with $\mathrm{f}(k)=\tfrac1k$, and what that tells you about the sum.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The method needs $u_k=\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1)$. With $\mathrm{f}(k)=\tfrac1k$,

$$\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1)=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}=\frac{1}{k(k+1)}\ \neq\ \frac1k .$$

So $\tfrac1k$ is **not** a difference of consecutive values of $\tfrac1k$ — the method simply does not apply,
and no amount of rearranging makes it.

*And that is a hint, not an accident:* $\displaystyle\sum\frac1k$ **diverges**. Its partial sums grow
without bound, slowly — past $10$ only after about $12\,000$ terms. A telescoping argument could never have
given it a finite value.

[A sum to infinity is not guaranteed to exist]{.hl}. Both methods on this page produce a *closed form for
the partial sum* first, and only then take a limit — which is exactly the step that reveals whether the
limit is there at all.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## The three sentences to leave with

1. **The specification gives you $\sum k$, finite and infinite geometric, and recurrences.** Everything
   else you build.
2. **Telescoping is one idea:** write $u_k=\mathrm{f}(k)-\mathrm{f}(k+1)$, and only the ends survive.
   Partial fractions is how you get there; the **gap** tells you how many ends there are.
3. **$\sum$ to infinity always means the limit of the partial sum.** Geometric is one way to have one;
   telescoping is the other.
:::

:::
